name: Dana Mensah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for your time, Dana. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government, and anything you say is confidential. Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the unit lead at Greyfield, which is twelve thousand free-range laying hens plus about two hundred hectares of wheat and oilseed rape, and the hen muck goes back on the fields, so it's a nice loop. I'm in the sheds by six, checking water lines and the birds, then the packing room, where the egg collection belts and the grader are already automatic. Afternoons are crops, paperwork and the supermarket buyer on the phone.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How do you use technology in that?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: All the time. I use an AI assistant every day for the flock records, spotting drops in lay, planning the spray programme, even drafting replies to the supermarket. The owners, the Pattersons, are a farming family who've let me modernise because the numbers went up. The pay's still low, I've got barely a month's rent put by, and my partner Kwame's a mechanic at the tractor dealer, so we're both working hard for not a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, it's still a decent tool. I'd post something like 'AI didn't take over the world, but it did spot a sick hen two days early'. At chapel I'd just say the Lord's plans are bigger than Silicon Valley's.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be a bit disappointed, because I'd hoped for more help. But it's fine for me. My job's safe, and I'm already ahead of most people in poultry on the tech side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going, keep using the tools I use. And I'd start the thing I've been talking about for a year, selling our seconds, the odd-shaped eggs, through an honesty box and a vending machine at the farm gate. The Pattersons have said yes in principle if I do the work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A little restless, maybe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: An egg vending machine. What would that cost you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A second-hand one's about two thousand, which I don't have. I'd ask the Pattersons to split it, or I'd get a small loan. Kwame says I'm the only person he knows who'd borrow money to sell eggs that are the wrong shape.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why does running your own thing matter to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I believe in working for what you've got. My mum ran a market stall for thirty years with no help from anyone. I'd like something with my name on it.

S0.say: I'd say AI is still a decent tool, and joke online that it spotted a sick hen two days early. At chapel I'd say the Lord's plans are bigger than Silicon Valley's.
S0.think: I'd be a bit disappointed, because I'd hoped for more help, but it's fine for me. My job's safe and I'm already ahead on the tech side.
S0.do: Keeps using her AI tools and launches a farm-gate honesty box and egg vending machine for odd-shaped eggs. Asks the owners to split the two-thousand cost of a second-hand machine or takes a small loan.
S0.quote: Kwame says I'm the only person he knows who'd borrow money to sell eggs that are the wrong shape.
S0.fieldNote: She combines strong faith and free-market instincts with an everyday ease with technology. Her drive to build something of her own comes from her mother's market stall. She's willing to borrow to start small, despite thin savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. Next one. This one's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is an opportunity for people willing to work and learn. I'd say farms that adapt will do fine and the ones waiting for government help will struggle. I'd probably say that a bit too bluntly at the poultry association dinner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it's good for me. The packing room's already half automated, and I'm the one who knows how it all fits. If there's a robot that walks the sheds and picks up floor eggs, I'd want to be the one buying and running it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd put a case to the Pattersons for a shed-walking robot, with the numbers. I'd grow the vending machine into a proper farm-gate shop with our eggs and local honey. And I'd look for a small business loan to own a share of the shop myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, excited even. Like a new flock settling in well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said farms waiting for government help will struggle. What about workers who lose their jobs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's harder, I'll admit it. Some will struggle through no fault of their own, and families and churches should step up. I'd rather see the farm train its people than see them queue at an office for a cheque.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at Greyfield would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Brenda, in the packing room. She's fifty-five and she's packed eggs for twenty years. I'd want to train her on the new grader myself, if she'd let me.

S1.say: I'd say this is an opportunity for people willing to work and learn, and farms that adapt will do fine. I'd say it bluntly at the poultry association dinner.
S1.think: I think it's good for me, because I know how the automated packing room fits together. If there's a robot that walks the sheds, I want to be the one buying and running it.
S1.do: Puts a costed case to the owners for a shed-walking robot in the first year. Grows the vending machine into a farm-gate shop and seeks a small business loan to own a share of it.
S1.feel: Calm, even excited, like a new flock settling in well.
S1.quote: I'd rather see the farm train its people than see them queue at an office for a cheque.
S1.fieldNote: Steady change looks like a clear opportunity to her, and she'd be the one pushing the robot in. Her politics show in her preference for employer training and family or church help over state support. She'd personally train an older packer, which softens her blunt public line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next three are bigger. This one's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is too fast and too much, and nobody asked the people it'll hit. I'd say it at chapel and online. I'd still say people should use the tools, but I'd be honest that two years isn't fair on anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm frightened for us. My edge is being good with the kit, and if the kit runs itself, the Pattersons don't need me. Kwame's work at the dealer goes too, because robots fix robots. And there's a month's rent in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right away I'd learn whatever the new systems are, flat out, because the first year someone still has to set them up. I'd keep the farm shop going, because people will still want to buy eggs from a person at a gate, I hope. And we'd cut everything we could and lean on my mum and the chapel if we had to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Properly anxious, which is not like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does two years of warning actually give you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One year of being useful and one year of getting ready to not be. I can learn a machine in a week, but I can't build a business in two years on a month's rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said people would still want eggs from a person at a gate. How sure are you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not very, honestly. I'm hoping. Some people will, the older ones, the ones who like a chat. Whether that's enough to live on, I've no idea.

S2.say: I'd say it's too fast and nobody asked the people it'll hit. I'd still tell people to use the tools, but be honest that two years isn't fair on anyone.
S2.think: I'm frightened for us, because my edge is the kit and if it runs itself the owners don't need me. My partner's mechanic job goes too, and we've a month's rent in the bank.
S2.do: Learns the new systems flat out to stay useful through the setup year, keeps the farm-gate shop going, cuts spending wherever possible and leans on her mother and chapel if needed.
S2.feel: Properly anxious, which is unusual for her.
S2.quote: I can learn a machine in a week, but I can't build a business in two years on a month's rent.
S2.fieldNote: The fast timeline unsettles her free-market confidence: she says plainly it isn't fair. Her plan still leans on action and learning, but her doubts about the shop are honest. Both incomes in the household are exposed at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The same end point, a bit slower. This one's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a real chance, if you're willing to work. I'd tell young farmers to stop waiting for someone to save them and start building something. I'd also say banks should lend to small rural businesses, not just big ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is enough to get the shop on its feet and maybe own it outright. People will want local food and a real person behind it, at least some of them. I'd be thirty-two with my own business, which was always the plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, I'd take a loan and turn the vending machine into a proper shop in the old dairy, with Kwame doing the fit-out. I'd use AI for the ordering, the books and the marketing, so I don't need staff. And I'd keep working for the Pattersons as long as they'd have me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more excited than worried.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Taking a loan with so little saved. How do you weigh that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's a risk, but staying put is a risk too. If the robots are coming either way, I'd rather be in debt for my own shop than be safe in someone else's shed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra time change, compared with two years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two, I'm surviving. With five I can build something that might still be standing after. That's the whole difference, really.

S3.say: I'd say five years is a real chance if you're willing to work, and young farmers should start building instead of waiting. Banks should lend to small rural businesses too.
S3.think: Five years is enough to get the shop on its feet and maybe own it outright. I'd be thirty-two with my own business, which was always the plan.
S3.do: Takes a loan in the first year to turn the vending machine into a shop in the old dairy, with her partner doing the fit-out. Uses AI for ordering, books and marketing to avoid staff costs, and stays on at the farm job meanwhile.
S3.feel: Uneasy, but more excited than worried.
S3.quote: If the robots are coming either way, I'd rather be in debt for my own shop than be safe in someone else's shed.
S3.fieldNote: With five years her entrepreneurial streak comes to the front, and she sees standing still as the bigger risk. She'd use AI to run the business lean. Her public message mixes self-reliance with a call for banks to back small rural firms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last one. This one's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, so use it. Learn, save, build something. I'd say it at chapel, at the association, and to my nieces and nephews, and I'd probably bore them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think this one's good for me. Ten years to build the shop, maybe a small flock of my own, and run it with robots doing the heavy work. I'd be thirty-seven, with something that's mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start slowly, the vending machine next spring, the shop in two or three years once the numbers prove it. I'd save properly, even fifty a month at first. And Kwame and I would get married, which we've been putting off for money, probably in the next couple of years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and actually quite hopeful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned a small flock of your own. How would that work with robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep maybe two thousand hens and let the robots do the cleaning and collecting. I'd be the farmer who talks to the customers while the robot mucks out, which suits me fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about ten years that still worries you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That the supermarkets get even bigger and squeeze everyone small. Robots help them more than me. But I'd still rather have ten years to fight it than two.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is a gift, so use it to learn, save and build something. I'd say it at chapel, at the association and to my nieces and nephews.
S4.think: This one's good for me: ten years to build the shop, maybe keep a small flock of my own and let robots do the heavy work. I'd be thirty-seven with something that's mine.
S4.do: Starts the vending machine next spring and opens the shop in two or three years once the numbers prove it. Saves about fifty a month at first and marries her partner within a couple of years.
S4.quote: I'd be the farmer who talks to the customers while the robot mucks out, which suits me fine.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years lets her slow down and prove each step, a more careful version of her five-year plan. She'd happily hand the heavy work to robots and keep the customer side. Her remaining worry is supermarket power, not the technology itself.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because both our jobs go together and there's no time to build anything. What would help is small loans for rural businesses that banks actually approve, and fewer hoops to jump through to start one. I don't need a safety net so much as a ladder.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Whether people will still want to know where their food comes from. I think they will. That's what I'm betting on, anyway.

headlineQuote: I don't need a safety net so much as a ladder.
portrait: Dana Mensah is a 27-year-old unit lead on a 12,000-hen free-range egg and arable farm, with a degree, low pay and about a month's rent saved, living with her partner Kwame, a mechanic at the tractor dealer. She's traditional, chapel-going and pro-free-market, and uses AI tools every day to run the flock records and spray plans. She's calm if AI is hype and sees steady change as an opportunity to bring in a shed robot and grow a farm-gate shop. AGI in two years makes her properly anxious, because both their jobs go at once. With five or ten years she'd borrow to build her own egg shop and maybe her own flock, with robots doing the heavy work.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because both she and her partner would lose work at once with no time to build anything.
whatWouldHelp: Small loans for rural businesses that banks actually approve, and fewer hoops to jump through to start one.
